lines: Four. Abraham Lincoln. Thanksgiving In Wartime.
On October 3rd, 1863, Lincoln issued the proclamation.
It was actually written by his Secretary of State, William Seward.
It set the last Thursday in November as a day of "Thanksgiving and Praise."
That year, it fell on November 26th.
Note the date.
October 3rd.
Same as Washington's, seventy-four years earlier.
This was the middle of the Civil War.
Both sides had been proclaiming their own days of thanksgiving, each asking for help in winning.
Lincoln's version urged one nation to restore peace and harmony.
From then on, presidents proclaimed it every year.
The holiday finally stuck.
Now.
The turkey.
There's a famous story that Lincoln's son, Tad, became attached to a turkey meant for the family's holiday dinner.
A turkey named Jack.
Tad begged his father to spare it.
And Lincoln did.
It was recorded by a White House reporter named Noah Brooks, in 1865.
Some call it the first turkey pardon.
Here's the catch.
It was a Christmas turkey, not a Thanksgiving one.
And the White House Historical Association says the idea that this started the pardon tradition is likely apocryphal.
So.
Did Jack live?
The story says yes.
Did he start a tradition?
No.
Scoreboard: Turkeys spared, one.
Possibly.
Asterisk.
Five. Ulysses S. Grant To Woodrow Wilson. The Poultry King.
In 1873, a Rhode Island turkey farmer named Horace Vose mailed a turkey to President Ulysses S.
Grant.
And then he did it again.
And again.
Every year.
Until his death in 1913.
Horace Vose was known as the "Poultry King."
He picked the bird himself, from the best flocks in Rhode Island and Connecticut.
His turkeys never weighed less than 30 pounds.
Some hit 50.
He slaughtered and dressed each one, put it in a box addressed to the president, and shipped it by express.
Four decades of presidents ate Horace's turkeys.
Horace did not do pardons.
In 1913, Woodrow Wilson got a rival bird from the Clerk of the House, a former Kentucky congressman named South Trimble.
Trimble's turkey weighed 30 pounds.
Vose's weighed 37.
Trimble claimed his tasted better, because it had been fed red peppers.
Which one did Wilson eat?
Nobody knows.
The Great Turkey Showdown of 1913 has no recorded winner.
Meanwhile, at the White House dinner table:
In 1878, after the Hayes family ate, they invited their cooks and staff to hold their own Thanksgiving dinner in the State Dining Room.
In 1897, Ida McKinley ordered a plain dinner: a 26-pound turkey, stuffed with oysters.
Plain, by 1897 standards.
And in 1912, William Howard Taft received a mince pie from his Aunt Delia.
Just in time for dinner.
Aunt Delia delivered.
Scoreboard: turkeys eaten, lots.
Spared, still one.
Asterisk.
Six. Woodrow Wilson. The War Years.
In 1917, America was in the First World War.
Food was being conserved for the war effort.
So Wilson's first wartime Thanksgiving followed the food conservation guidelines.
And left out the cranberries.
No cranberries.
That's how you know it was serious.
A year later, the war was over.
Days after the armistice, Wilson's 1918 proclamation said: "God has in His good pleasure given us peace."
Cranberries presumably returned.
